en: The vessels were human vessels;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra was the father of the Kauravas.
Bhaṭa: Jayatrāta, the messenger.
Duryodhana: The Kuru king.
Duḥśāsana: The younger brother of the Kuru king.
Śakuni—the maternal uncle of the Kuru king.
Ghaṭotkaca—the Rākṣasa son of Bhīma, who has arrived as an envoy.
Female roles.
Gāndhārī—mother of the Kauravas.
Duḥśalā—sister of the Kauravas and wife of Jayadratha.
Pratīhārī—female doorkeeper.
A Play (At the conclusion of the benediction, the Stage Manager enters). Stage Manager:

May Nārāyaṇa, the sole refuge of the three worlds, who provides the means through hundreds of stratagems for the gods, and who is the director (sūtradhāra) who both introduces and concludes the continuous drama of the three worlds, protect you. (1)
(Walking about) Thus I address the noble gentlemen. Ah! While I am occupied in making this request, what is this sound that is heard? Well, I shall look.
(Offstage) Ho there! Let it be announced, let it be announced at once!

Sūtradhāra: Let it be known. This is indeed Prince Abhimanyu, who, while Janārdana was assisting Dhananjaya against the host of the Saṃśaptakas, was surrounded and struck down by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who were incensed by the subsequent slaughter of Bhīṣma. For they are fleeing, terrified of Arjuna’s counter-attack.
From that point on, the kings of men, gazing toward that direction, returned to their own dwellings with their senses lost,
marked by the arrows of Subhadrā’s son.

(Then enters a soldier. Soldier: Ho there! Let it be announced to the Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra—whose kinsmen are praised by a hundred sons, and whose long vision is extended by discipline and conduct broadened through wisdom—that this warrior, having agitated the army of kings with the slaughter of chariots, horses, and elephants...
By that very deed which was displayed with ease by the child Arjuna in battle,
that son of Subhadrā was suddenly lifted into the lap of Indra, the grandfather, in the sky amidst hundreds of kings who had rushed forward from all sides in the fray. || 3 ||
(Then enter Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī, Duḥśalā, and the female doorkeeper.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Alas, how is this?
Who has committed this offense against the path of my hearing?
Who is this that speaks unpleasant words to me, whom he calls his own dear one?
Who is it that, fearless, proclaims the destruction of our lineage, which is already stained by the sin of killing children? || 4 ||
Gāndhārī: Great King! It is known, however, that a family conflict will arise which will result in the destruction of our sons.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Gāndhārī, it is known. Gāndhārī: Great King, when indeed?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: O Gāndhārī, listen!
Today, provoked by the slaughter of Abhimanyu, with Kṛṣṇa holding the reins and the whip in his hand, he is filled with indignation.
Pārtha, aided by that wielder of the fierce bow, will accomplish it; thus the world, having met its destruction, will come to rest. || 5 ||

Gāndhārī: Alas, my child Abhimanyu! Even while such a family conflict, which brings about the destruction of men, was underway, you, by the turn of our fate, were sinking into the state of childhood; where have you gone now, my grandson?
Duḥśalā: He who has now bestowed widowhood upon his daughter-in-law Uttarā has likewise ordained widowhood for his own circle of young women.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Then by whom was this causeway built across the ocean of calamity? Soldier: Your Majesty, by me!
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Who are you?
Bhaṭa: Great King! I am indeed Jayatrāta.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Jayatrāta!
By whom was Abhimanyu slain? Whose life is now a source of grief?
By whom has the very self of the five Pāṇḍava fires been turned into fuel? (6)

Soldier: Great King! It is said that Prince Abhimanyu was slain by many kings who had assembled together; Jayadratha, however, must have been the instrumental cause. Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Alas, Jayadratha was the instrumental cause!
Soldier: Great King, indeed so it is.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Alas, Jayadratha has been slain!
(Hearing this, Duḥśalā weeps.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Who is this that weeps?
Doorkeeper: Great King! It is the princess Duḥśalā.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Child, enough, enough with weeping! Look, your husband surely does not approve of your perpetual widowhood.
By whom his own self was made the target of Gāṇḍīva’s arrows.
Duḥśalā: Therefore, father, please grant me leave; I too shall go to the presence of my daughter-in-law Uttarā. Dhṛtarāṣṭra: My child, what will you say?
Duḥśalā: Father, I shall say this: "I too shall observe your assumption of this disguise from this day forward."

Gāndhārī: My daughter! Do not, do not speak such inauspicious words! Your husband truly lives. Duḥśalā: Mother! Whence could I have such fortune? For who indeed would live after having done what is displeasing to Dhanañjaya, who has Janārdana as his ally?

Dhṛtarāṣṭra: The ascetic Duḥśalā has spoken the truth. For what reason? He who was long reared in the lap fashioned by the eight arms of Kṛṣṇa as his pillow, and who is the second intoxication out of affection for the intoxicated Halāyudha.
Having slain him who was the vessel of affection for the sons of Pṛthā, whose prowess is equal to that of the gods—who here will obtain to live long on account of his own evil deeds? (8)
Victory to you! Now, having seen his son in such a state, what did that wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow do?
Bhaṭa: Great King, was this event that occurred in the presence of Arjuna?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: How is it that even Arjuna was not there?
Soldier: Great King, indeed so it is.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: How has this event transpired?
Soldier: Listen—while Dhanañjaya, accompanied by Janārdana, was engaged with the host of Saṃśaptakas, Prince Abhimanyu, who had not yet seen the faults of battle due to his youth, entered the fray.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Ah, his death is indeed most fitting. For who is able to venture into a cave where a tiger is present? Now, what are the remaining Pāṇḍavas doing?
Soldier: Great King, please listen.
They have not yet placed his body upon the funeral pyre themselves, so that they may behold Arjuna.
And they recorded the names of those lords of men by whom he was struck upon his body.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Gāndhārī! Come, then; let us go to the very bank of the Gaṅgā. Gāndhārī: Great King! Indeed, let us bathe there. Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Gāndhārī! Listen.
This very day, I shall offer water to your sons who have been slain through their own transgression;
yet I am not capable of [reviving them] by means of the offerings of water.
to besiege the encampment of the kings. || 10 ||
(Then enter Duryodhana, Duḥśāsana, and Śakuni.
Duryodhana: Dear Duḥśāsana! Since the death of Abhimanyu, our enmity has become fixed.
Victory has been attained, the enemies have been shaken and cast down;
the pride of this slayer of Madhu has been uprooted,
and today I have gained renown along with prosperity.

Duḥśāsana: Alas! Indeed, the sons of Pāṇḍu have been hemmed in after Jayadratha’s force was overcome and the second Arjuna [Abhimanyu] was struck down by hundreds of arrows while Saubhadra was falling.
And having encountered these calamities today in battle due to Bhīṣma’s fall, we have indeed shot fierce arrows of grief into their hearts by the destruction of their sons. (12)
Śakuni said: "Today Jayadratha has displayed great prowess in battle, an achievement unimagined by other kings,
in that he has forcibly overcome them in combat."
His incomparable fame was snatched away by his son, who was his equal. || 13 ||
Duryodhana: Uncle! This way, please! Duḥśāsana! This way, please! We shall pay our respects to our venerable father.
Śakuni: Dear Duryodhana, do not speak thus! Granted, this family feud was not to his liking, and he reproaches us because of his affection for the Pāṇḍavas.
For, having achieved victory in battle and being equal in form [to him], they should approach him with faces full of joy. || 14 ||
Duryodhana: Uncle! Not so, not so! Let it be as it may; we shall pay our respects to our venerable father. Both: Very well. (They walk about.
Duryodhana: Father! I, Duryodhana, pay my respects.
Duḥśāsana: Father! I, Duḥśāsana, salute you. Śakuni: I, Śakuni, salute you.
All: Why is no word of blessing being offered?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "O son! How can this be called a benediction?
When the young son of Subhadrā has been slain, and Kṛṣṇa and Pārtha have no regard for their own lives, how can a blessing be offered?"
Duryodhana: Father, what is the cause of this agitation?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: What is the cause of this agitation?
There is but one woman in this family, who has many sons as her lords.
This daughter obtained, who is superior even to a hundred sons—
through your favor toward her kinsmen, she would otherwise have met with the ignoble state of widowhood. (16)
Duryodhana: Father! And what of Jayadratha in this matter?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: It is said that the Pāṇḍavas were held captive by him, who was clever in seeking boons.
Duryodhana: Ah! Held captive by him? But surely they were held by many others as well!
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Oh! Alas!
How is it that the arms of so many assembled men, who were pitiless-souled as they struck at their young son, did not fall off? 17.
Duryodhana: Father!
Having slain the aged Bhīṣma by deceitful means, will their arms not fall?
Having slain him of unchildlike prowess, they shall fall [themselves]. 18.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: My child! Is the fall of Bhīṣma equal to the slaughter of Abhimanyu?
Duryodhana: Father! How could it not be equal?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Son! Listen.
Bhīṣma was indeed slain with his death at his own will, having attained self-satisfaction through his own instruction;
but this youth, the lord of the Kuru lineage, has been cut down—the very first sprout of Arjuna.
Duḥśāsana: Father! He is a child, not a fool! Abhimanyu— Dhṛtarāṣṭra: What, what does Duḥśāsana say?
Duḥśāsana: Indeed so!
While all of us were looking on and fighting,
he took up his bow in his hand, heated by the exertion,
as if it had been approached by the very rays of the sun.
All the protectors of the earth were marked with arrows. || 20 ||
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Alas, oh! By one boy alone—by the son of Subhadrā—such a thing has been done!
What will Pārtha do to you, tormented as he is by the calamity of his sons? || 21 ||
Duryodhana: What will he do?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: He will do that which you shall see with your remaining lifespan.
Duryodhana: Father! Who is this so-called Arjuna?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: My son! You do not even know Arjuna? Duryodhana: Father! I do not know him.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Then indeed, I too do not know him. However, there are many who know Arjuna’s strength and prowess; ask them.
Duryodhana: Father! Why should I ask those who know Arjuna’s strength and prowess?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Son, listen!
Ask Śakra, whom he formerly honored with the sacrifice of his own life-force when the Nivātakavacas were slain.
Ask Hara, who assumed the form of a Kirāta and was gratified by various kinds of questions;
ask him who, as Agni, accepted the offering of serpents and was satisfied at Khāṇḍava; and ask Citrāṅgada, by whom you were conquered today and who is protected by his knowledge.
Duryodhana: If this is Arjuna’s prowess, are there no warriors in our army who can oppose Arjuna?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: My son, who are they?
Duryodhana: Surely Karna alone is enough.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Oh, poor Karṇa is indeed laughable!
Duryodhana: For what reason?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Listen.
Deprived of his armor by Śakra, rendered a mere half-charioteer, negligent,
having obtained his weapons in vain through deception, and full of compassion—
Karna will indeed become the equal of Arjuna.
If Agni, Indra, and Rudra are the preceptors in the granting of weapons... || 23 ||
Śakuni: You are capable of making us lose heart.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Śakuni speaks thus. O Śakuni! Indeed, whatever deeds have been performed by you, who are ever devoted to gambling—
The fire of enmity in this family does not subside, even toward children. (24)
Duryodhana: Ah! This earthquake, accompanied by a roar, has suddenly arisen from where? And the sky seems as if set ablaze by falling meteors.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: O son! I think thus:
clearly seeing his grandson slain, the tears of Mahendra fall like meteors, for his mind is deeply distressed. 26.
Duryodhana: Jayatrāta! Go; find out what this sound is that has arisen in the Pāṇḍava camp, mingled with the blare of conchs and drums and the roar of lions.

Soldier: As you command. (Exit and re-enter) Victory to the Great King! Dhananjaya, having returned from repelling the host of the Saṃśaptakas, has slain his son while he was still in his father’s lap; and having bathed him with tears, he has made a vow, provoked as he is by Janārdana. Duryodhana: What? What did he say? What did he say?

The Soldier: With hearts satisfied by that very resolve, and with faces beaming with joy as they witnessed the victory achieved by those who were eager for his prowess, a sudden roar was let out in exultation.
At that moment, the earth—already burdened by the weight of the great and best of mountains, and now agitated by kings—trembled like a young woman seized by a fit of panic.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: This earth trembles by the mere strength of his vow;
it is quite evident that when his bow is touched, the three worlds will shake. (28)
Duryodhana: O Jayatrāta! What was promised by him?
Soldier: "By whomsoever my son has been slain, and those others who have gone to their death, I shall slay them all tomorrow when the sun has reached its setting. (29)
Duryodhana: What is the expiation for the violation of a vow?

Soldier: It is said to be ascending the funeral pyre together with the Gāṇḍīva bow. Duryodhana: Uncle! Ascending the pyre! Ascending the pyre! Dear Duḥśāsana! Ascending the pyre! Ascending the pyre! We too shall now exert ourselves to fulfill our vow.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: My son! What will you do? Duryodhana: Indeed, I shall cover Jayadratha with the entire multitude of all the akṣauhiṇīs; moreover, according to the instruction of Droṇa, I shall—
He shall arrange an impenetrable formation;
those [enemies], their hearts exhausted along with their elephants and warriors,
and their desires unfulfilled, shall enter the fire.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Even if he has entered the earth or ascended to the vault of heaven, those arrows of him whose eye is Kṛṣṇa will pursue him everywhere. (31)
The soldier: Anyone else who should speak thus to the king, who is so cruel and whose commands are ever-ready for execution, would not live for even a moment.
(Then Ghaṭotkaca enters.
Ghaṭotkaca: Ho there!
Here I go, urged on by the desire to destroy the son of Subhadrā.
Desiring today to behold the enemy of ignoble mind,
he reflected upon the command of the Wielder of the Discus, just as a lordly elephant, wary of the goad, reflects upon the tribute [of his keeper].

(Looking down) Here is the door to his reception hall. I shall now descend. (Having descended) I shall announce myself by my own name. Ho there! I am Ghaṭotkaca, the son of Hiḍimbā; having received the command of the Lord of the Yadus, I have come. My preceptor must be seen here by me—he who, through the faults of his own conduct, has become an enemy.
Duryodhana: Come, come! Enter the enemy's palace; my curiosity is great.
Let me hear boldly the words of Janārdana; here stands Duryodhana.

Ghaṭotkaca: (Entering) Ah! Here is the venerable Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the progenitor of a hundred ignoble sons. Indeed, what a wonderful distinction of form—both graceful and profound! How marvelous, how marvelous! Though old, his skin is not wrinkled and his shoulders are thickly set; he possesses a credible appearance through the stability of his hundred sons.
I believe this venerable man was created by the gods, who, fearing for the protection of the triple heaven, fashioned him with a face closed in apprehension. 35.

(Approaching) Grandfather! I salute you, Ghaṭotkaca—(having spoken thus far) No, no! This is not out of order. Yudhiṣṭhira and the others, who are my elders, salute you first; afterwards, I, Ghaṭotkaca, salute you. Dhṛtarāṣṭra: Come, come, my son!
This sorrow is not dear to me either.
Since your soul is pained by the loss of your brothers,
this purpose of yours has not been fulfilled;
thus, because of the fault of my son, I have been rendered miserable.

Ghaṭotkaca: Oh, how truly auspicious is this venerable one! The Blessed One who wields the discus has called you the grandfather, the source of all that is auspicious. Dhṛtarāṣṭra: (Rising from his seat) What does the Blessed One who wields the discus command?
Ghaṭotkaca: No, no, no! You must listen to Janārdana’s message while remaining seated upon your throne.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra: As the Blessed One, whose weapon is the discus, commands. (He sits down.

Ghaṭotkaca: Grandfather! Listen! Alas, dear Abhimanyu! Alas, dear lamp of the Kuru lineage! Alas, dear sprout of the Yadu clan! Having abandoned both your mother and me, your maternal uncle, you have departed for heaven with the hope of beholding your grandfather. Grandfather! If this is the state of Arjuna due to the loss of his only son, what indeed will be yours? Therefore, quickly restore your strength now.
"So that the fire arising from your grief for your son may not consume the sacrificial offering consisting of his life-breaths.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: "This was uttered by Kṛṣṇa with wrathful resolve;
indeed, I see the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow already intent upon the slaughter of all the Kṣatriyas. (37)
All: Oh, what a ridiculous statement! Ghaṭotkaca: Why is this being laughed at? Duryodhana: This is what is being laughed at.
That Kṛṣṇa, having conceived envy, consults with the gods—
he who believes that the entire circle of kings has been slain by Pārtha alone.
Ghaṭotkaca said: You laugh, while I am the speaker sent by the wielder of the discus;
this report of Pārtha’s deeds was made known to you, yet alas, it is indeed appropriate for you alone! (39)
Moreover, you too must listen to the message of Janārdana.
Duḥśāsana: Wait a moment, O despiser of Kṣatriyas!
He whose command is upheld on earth by all the kings—
No other message shall even be heard in the presence of that king.

Ghaṭotkaca: How does Duḥśāsana speak? O Duḥśāsana! Is Cakrāyudha (Kṛṣṇa) not indeed your king—he by whom kings were formerly released from old age with their pride and exaltation shattered, and who, while the circle of monarchs looked on, struck down Bhīṣma from his outstretched hand when he had become unworthy?
How is it that King Cakrāyudha is not praiseworthy for you—he in whose bedchamber Fortune dwells, ever ready to fulfill his commands, while he himself is the most eminent among kings? 41.
Duryodhana: Duḥśāsana! Enough with this dispute!
Whether he be a king or not a king, whether he be strong or weak—what is the use of saying more in this matter? What does your lord say? (42)

Ghaṭotkaca: Indeed! Indeed! The Lord himself, the Blessed One whose weapon is the discus, is the sovereign of the three worlds; he is especially our own lord. Moreover, know that the destruction of the Kṣatriyas is at an end;
let there be lightness for the earth through the defeat of hundreds of kings.
For indeed, compared to the discharge of fierce weapons raised at the head of battle due to the destruction of his son, nothing is too great a burden for Phalguna.
Śakuni said: "If this earth were conquered by mere words, or if with every word the slaughter of all the Kṣatriyas were accomplished," (44)
Ghaṭotkaca: Hey! Hey! This Śakuni speaks. O Śakuni!
Cast aside the dice, Śakuni! In the work of battle, a chessboard (aṣṭāpada) suited for Kuru arrows is more appropriate.
Here there is no abduction of wives, nor any matter of kingship; here the stakes are life itself, with passion for fierce strength and arrows.
Duryodhana: Ho there! You have returned to your natural state;
you speak harshly, casting aside authority and disregarding everything as you speak with long-reaching arrogance.
If indeed you have such pride in the fierce nature of your maternal kin, we too are indeed formidable, possessing the fierce disposition of Rākṣasas. || 46 ||
Ghaṭotkaca: Peace, peace! May evil be averted! Even among the Rākṣasas, you yourselves are far more cruel. Why?
For the night-stalkers did not burn their brothers while they slept in the house of lac; nor did the night-stalkers lay hands upon the wife of a brother in such a manner.
Moreover, those night-stalkers do not remember to kill a son in battle;
though they possess deformed bodies and fierce conduct, they are not devoid of compassion. (47)
Duryodhana: You are indeed a messenger who has arrived; you have not come for the purpose of battle.
Take your message and depart; we do not kill messengers.
Ghaṭotkaca: (With anger) Why do you insult me as if I were a messenger? Stop, sir! I am no messenger. Enough of your resolve; strike, for I have been struck!
I am not the weak Abhimanyu standing here, for my bowstring has been severed.
This is my great and youthful ambition. Moreover, here stands Ghaṭotkaca with his lips bitten and fist raised;
let some man arise who would wish to go to this abode.
(All rise.

Dhṛtarāṣṭra: O grandson Ghaṭotkaca! May you forgive me, may you forgive me! Be one who heeds my word. Ghaṭotkaca: Enough, enough! I have been summoned by the words of my grandfather. Nevertheless, I am unable to restrain my wrath. What should the venerable Nārāyaṇa be informed?
Duryodhana: Enough! To whom should this be reported? He should be told these words from my very lips:
"Why do you speak so much in vain? We are certainly not to be subdued by your harshness; you ought not to say anything out of anger.
When you give me battle, I shall go forth surrounded by a continuous canopy of hundreds of royal umbrellas; stay here with the Pāṇḍavas, for I will give you my reply with my arrows. (41)
Ghaṭotkaca: Grandfather! Here I go. Dhṛtarāṣṭra: My grandson! Go, go!
Ghaṭotkaca: O kings! Listen to the final message from Janārdana.
Practice righteousness, show regard for your own kin,
and accomplish here everything that you desire in your heart;
you who bear the form of a Pāṇḍava, like one whose instruction is innate.
Kṛtānta will come upon you together with the rays of the sun. || 52 ||
(All exit.
The interlude named "The Messenger Ghaṭotkaca" is finished.
